title: Separate extreme-injustice invalidity from institutional moral limits and defective law
author: Worldview Sorter jurisprudence review
currentBehavior: Release 1.20 assigns PLI073@1 but omits PLI072@1 on Full. Its moral-limits rule remains not_measured. PLI072@1 does not exclude institutionally incorporated moral limits, and PLI073@1 treats defective_law as invalidity support. Source-based-validity also opposes PLI073:not_law, conflating an extreme threshold with denial that ordinary immoral laws can remain valid.
proposedBehavior: Publish PLI072@2 and PLI073@2 for the exact proposition below. PLI073@2 specifies satisfaction of all accepted institutional validity criteria, no institutional moral limits, and intolerable extreme injustice rather than ordinary unfairness. PLI072 agreement and PLI073:not_law support; PLI072 disagreement and PLI073:valid_but_unjust oppose. defective_law and depends are nondirectional. Preserve two distinct units in each direction. MCP-2026-097 separately reviews ordinary immoral-law evidence; this proposal does not infer a whole philosophical tradition.
rationale: Procedural enactment alone does not exclude inclusive-positivist moral invalidity. Focal moral defectiveness also does not settle technical legal validity. Explicit institutional and threshold stipulations isolate the narrow invalidity question without turning moral disobedience or ordinary injustice into a legal-status answer.

philosophicalBasis.proposition: Extreme injustice can make an enactment legally invalid independently of the system's accepted institutional criteria.
neighboringViews: Inclusive positivism permits moral validity criteria when institutionally incorporated; agreement with such criteria is not independent invalidity.
Exclusive positivism separates moral merits from source-based validity.
Finnis-style focal defectiveness can coexist with technical legal validity.
A moral reason not to obey or apply a law does not alone establish legal invalidity.
nonEntailments: Ordinary immoral laws cannot remain legally valid.
Defective law necessarily lacks technical legal validity.
A duty to obey, enforce, or resist any particular enactment.
A natural-law, religious, or political identity assignment.
philosophicalBasis.existingGap: One assigned unit cannot measure this two-unit rule. The successor adds PLI072@2 and revises PLI073@2 without transferring old answers to new wording. Likely false positives from incorporated constitutional moral tests, defective-law terminology, and moral disobedience are explicitly excluded.
philosophicalBasis.scholarlyDisagreement: The reviewed SEP Natural Law Theories sections 3.1.1 and 4 distinguish higher-law reasoning from incorporated moral rules, discuss denial of legal character for sufficiently grave injustice, and also preserve discourse-dependent technical validity. The entry acknowledges disagreement among Alexy, Finnis and others. This is support for a contested narrow proposition, not consensus or an exhaustive statement of Radbruch's formula.

sourceClaims.claim: Finnis, Natural Law Theories, sections 3.1.1 and 4, distinguishes higher-law reasoning independent of institutional incorporation and discusses sufficiently grave injustice as grounds for denying legal character. Section 4 separately allows technical validity and defective or non-central law; defectiveness alone therefore does not settle the target proposition.

Legal Positivism, introduction and section 4.1, presents law's existence as dependent on social facts rather than merits and distinguishes moral fallibility from positivism itself. Moral condemnation alone need not establish legal invalidity or a duty to obey.
Bibliographic lead for the extreme-injustice threshold debate; the primary text was not read in this review. No direct-text verification or item validation is claimed.
Bibliographic lead for the injustice argument discussed in the reviewed SEP synthesis; this monograph was not read in this review.
Bibliographic lead for focal-sense legal analysis. The reviewed evidence here is Finnis's SEP section 4, not a claimed reading of this book.
Bibliographic lead for the separation debate. This article was not read in this review; the modest separation and moral-fallibility claims rely on the reviewed SEP entries.

alternatives: Admit PLI072@1 unchanged: rejected because institutional moral limits remain a false positive.
Treat defective_law as support or opposition: rejected because it does not settle technical invalidity.
Reduce the two-unit gate: rejected; the successor supplies a second explicit unit instead.
